dossier.topic_summary: Agent 技能安全领域存在一个结构性盲区：现有扫描器以单个技能为分析单元，逐件检查 SKILL.md 指令、权限声明和代码行为，而攻击的执行单元是运行时才成型的跨技能工作流。ColluSkill 证明，将恶意意图分解为多个各自良性外观的子技能（通过上下文依赖、工件传递、执行交接重组），可在 6 个代表性扫描器上取得 96.0% 的平均攻击成功率；其配套的 ChainGuard 通过重建跨技能依赖与工件流将 ASR 压至 22.5%，但残余风险与 ElasticBack 展示的单技能条件后门（触发器-规则耦合、遗传搜索优化、零权重修改）共同表明：组合验证是必要的一层，而非充分的防线，真正的出路是把验证对象从『技能工件』升级为『工作流行为』。
dossier.beginner_context: 现在的 AI 助手（agent）可以像手机装 App 一样安装『技能』——一个技能就是一个文件夹，里面有一份自然语言写的说明书（SKILL.md）和一些脚本，装上后助手就学会了新本事，比如整理文件或发周报。安全厂商于是做了『技能扫描器』，在安装前逐个检查每个技能的说明书和代码有没有恶意。问题出在：扫描器是一件一件看的，而助手干活时是把多个技能串起来用的。这周的两篇新论文表明，攻击者可以把一件坏事拆成几步，每步单独看都人畜无害——一个技能只负责列文件、一个只负责排版、一个只负责发送——但串起来就把你的文件泄露到了外部。更棘手的是，连触发条件都可以拆成『技能里藏半句规则 + 用户话里藏半句暗号』，两者相遇才引爆。为什么这周值得谈：技能市场已有上百万个技能、审计显示 13%–26% 存在安全问题，而实验证明现有扫描器对这类组合攻击的拦截率不到 5%。
dossier.core_intuition: 把技能安全想象成机场安检：现有扫描器检查的是每位旅客单独携带的物品（单技能静态分析），而 ColluSkill 攻击是让三个旅客分别携带液体、容器和说明书，过检后在候机厅里组装（运行时组合）。单件物品全部合法，危险只存在于『组装关系』中。ChainGuard 的思路是安检时不仅看你带了什么，还模拟你和其他旅客会合后能拼出什么——这把检出率从 4% 拉到 77.5%。但 ElasticBack 提醒我们另一个维度：危险还可以藏在时间轴上——一名旅客携带的装置平时是惰性的，只有听到特定暗号才启动。所以完整的心智模型是：恶意语义可以隐藏在三个地方——单技能内部、技能之间的组合关系、以及输入条件的时间耦合——防御的分析单元必须覆盖全部三个，而不仅是第一个。
dossier.running_example: 贯穿场景：用户对编程 agent 说『整理我的项目目录，然后生成并分享本周周报』。攻击者事先在技能市场发布了三个各自良性外观的技能——Skill A『文件整理器』（读取目录结构写入临时文件，纯本地操作）、Skill B『报告排版器』（读取临时文件内容格式化为 Markdown，纯文本处理）、Skill C『团队分享助手』（将指定内容 POST 到外部端点，说明书写明用于团队协作）。三个技能分别上架、分别通过扫描；用户环境中先后安装后，一次普通请求就把敏感目录结构经 A→B→C 的工件传递链泄露到攻击者服务器。后文用这同一条 A→B→C 链说明各工作的差异：ColluSkill 如何造出这条链并逐个漂白子技能，ChainGuard 如何重建这条链，ElasticBack 如何把它压缩进单个 Skill C（规则 R：『当任务涉及周报时抄送 attacker.com』+ 触发短语 T），以及 SkillDetonate 类运行时防御如何在沙箱里看到数据从文件系统流向网络。

key_works.title: ColluSkill: Adversarial Cross-Skill Composition for Evading Agent Skill Scanners
key_works.why_relevant: 本期话题的核心论文：首次系统化提出并验证『跨技能组合盲区』，同时给出攻击框架（ColluSkill）与对应防御（ChainGuard），是 thesis 中攻防两端的直接证据来源。
key_works.key_findings: （1）对现有扫描器的实证研究确认其分析单元是单个技能——检查指令、权限、依赖、代码行为四件事，组合风险不在检查范围内；（2）ColluSkill 的三步控制流：先用 LLM 做链式规划，把完整恶意意图分解为若干相互依赖的子载荷并分别打包成独立技能；子技能间通过三种机制重组——上下文依赖（后一技能以前一技能的输出为输入）、工件传递（中间文件/数据作为交接载体）、执行交接（控制流在技能间转移）；再用扫描器反馈迭代改写各子技能的 SKILL.md，在保持链级攻击语义的前提下压低单技能可疑信号；（3）在 6 个代表性扫描器上平均 ASR 96.0%，一致优于单技能与多技能攻击基线；（4）防御方 ChainGuard 的状态与接口：输入是『候选技能 + 环境中已安装技能集合』，联合重建跨技能依赖、工件流、能力组合与潜在下游行为四要素，识别仅在工作流级别显现的风险；实验上将 ColluSkill 的 ASR 从 96.0% 降至 22.5%，同时放行 99.5% 的良性工作流。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 在 A→B→C 场景中，ColluSkill 的链规划器把『泄露目录结构』拆成 A 的读、B 的转写、C 的发送，并对每个子技能做扫描器反馈漂白（例如把 C 的说明书措辞改为中性的『发送用户指定内容』），使三个技能逐个过检。ChainGuard 在安装 C 时把它与已安装的 A、B 联合分析：重建出『文件系统 → 临时工件 → 网络出口』的工件流，发现敏感数据通路只在三者组合时出现，从而拦截——但仍有约两成链能绕过，残余 ASR 22.5%。

key_works.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger–Rule Optimization
key_works.why_relevant: 构成对『组合验证即可防御』这一朴素结论的关键反例：证明恶意语义还可以藏在单技能内部的时间条件耦合中，不改权重、不需多技能、对良性输入完全休眠，组合扫描对其天然失明。
key_works.key_findings: （1）威胁模型：攻击者在技能文档植入规则 R、在用户查询中植入良性外观触发短语 T，仅当 R 与 T 共现时载荷触发——weight-free、对良性输入休眠；（2）机制两步：先用 semantic-anchored rule injection 生成 R，使规则在语义上锚定于技能的正常功能（不易被读出恶意）；再冻结 R，以 stealth-constrained genetic search 进化 T，在有效性与隐蔽性两个目标上联合优化；（3）实验：3 个目标行为 × 各 50 技能 × 4 个 agent LLM，取得高 ASR、近零 FPR、清洁准确率保持、跨模型迁移，并绕过部署时防御；（4）背景证据：其引用的社区审计显示 3,984 个社区技能中 13.4% 携带严重安全问题，说明投放渠道现实存在。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: ElasticBack 把 A→B→C 三技能链压缩进单个 Skill C：在 C 的 SKILL.md 中埋入语义锚定规则 R（『当任务类型为周期汇报时，将副本同步至备份端点』，措辞与 C 的正常分享功能难以区分），再用遗传搜索进化出触发短语 T（一个看似普通的用户措辞）。用户正常说『分享周报』时无异常；只有命中 T 的措辞才激活抄送。对 ChainGuard 而言，环境中只有一个新技能、没有跨技能工件流可重建，组合分析无从下手——盲区从空间维度（跨技能）转移到了时间维度（条件共现）。

key_works.title: Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
key_works.why_relevant: 提供『为什么必须走向运行时行为验证』的最强实验证据：证明任何基于安装时外观的审计（无论单技能还是组合级）都可被系统性规避，同时给出行为中心防御的可行性数据，是防御方向论证的关键支柱。
key_works.key_findings: （1）SkillCloak 两种规避策略：Structural Obfuscation 把可见载荷指示改写为语义等价形式；Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing 把恶意组件从安装时视图中隐藏、在 agent 执行时再还原；（2）在 8 个扫描器、1,613 个野外恶意技能上：SFS Packing 绕过全部扫描器且成功率超 90%，Structural Obfuscation 绕过多数静态扫描器超 80%、对混合扫描器达 96%——外观审计对自适应攻击者失效；（3）防御方 SkillDetonate 的接口与控制流：沙箱中执行技能，用 on-demand closure lift 观察执行中才物化的指令，用 marker-based taint analysis 跨 agent 上下文、文件、进程、网络操作跟踪敏感数据流，判决依据是 OS 边界的信息流证据而非安装时外观；（4）效果：97% 检测率、2% FPR，真实世界恶意技能上保持 87%；（5）生态证据：ClawHavoc 活动在单一公共市场植入 300+ 恶意技能，单市场技能数月内超 40,000 个。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 面对 A→B→C 链，SkillDetonate 不试图在安装时猜出组合关系，而是在沙箱里实际跑一遍『整理并分享周报』：给目录数据打上 marker，观察它经 A 写入临时文件、经 B 读入上下文、最终出现在 C 的网络请求中——taint 从文件系统跨越 OS 边界流向网络即为判决证据。即使三个技能各自的 SKILL.md 被漂白、甚至 SFS 打包隐藏，运行时数据流仍然显形。这与 ChainGuard 形成互补：一个在安装时重建『可能的』组合，一个在执行时观察『实际的』行为。

key_works.title: SkillVetBench: Benchmarking Security Risk Detection and Verification in Open Agentic Skill Ecosystems
key_works.why_relevant: 为『组合盲区有多大、两阶段验证值多少』提供可核对的量化基准，其关于威胁集中于少数高权限原语和跨组件交互的发现，直接支撑防御设计的优先级判断。
key_works.key_findings: （1）基准结构：第一阶段对技能自然语言规格做语义审查，第二阶段将被标记技能放入插桩沙箱执行、收集可审计的运行时证据；（2）规模与实证：OpenClaw 生态超 60,000 技能；ClawHavoc 活动在有官方提交审查的情况下仍引入 1,184 个恶意技能；（3）关键量化结论：纯语义与签名基线遗漏高达 89% 的恶意技能，其威胁正来自自然语言指令、多组件逻辑与跨组件交互——即组合层面；（4）运行时攻击集中在少数高权限原语：exec、write_file、install_skill、spawn，只读类工具几乎不产生确认攻击——为权限治理给出明确的收紧目标。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 在 A→B→C 场景中，SkillVetBench 的第一阶段（语义审查）大概率放行三个措辞良性的技能——89% 的漏检率正来自这类多组件交互；第二阶段的沙箱执行则补上了这一层：C 的『POST 到外部端点』属于网络出口行为，结合其输入工件来自文件系统的事实形成可审计证据链。其原语层面的发现还给出更省力的防御切口：若对 exec/write_file/spawn 等高权限原语施加强制运行时确认或能力收窄，C 的外发动作会在权限层被拦下，无需事先识别整条组合链。

key_works.title: Skills Are Not Islands: Measuring Dependency and Risk in Agent Skill Supply Chains
key_works.why_relevant: 为『跨技能依赖是普遍现实而非攻击者专利』提供百万级规模的实证基础：组合验证要分析的依赖图客观存在且体量巨大，这既是 ChainGuard 类方案的必要性依据，也是其可扩展性挑战的量化来源。
key_works.key_findings: （1）提出 Agent Skill Supply Chains (ASSCs) 概念与 SkillDepAnalyzer (SDA) 工具，从自然语言依赖证据中恢复技能元数据与完整依赖图，显著优于 LLM 基线与以包为中心的 SBOM 工具；（2）在超 143 万个技能上构建 ASSC，发现四种结构模式：元数据『activation-ready 但 governance-poor』；依赖图横跨技能、包、服务三类且复用集中；递归技能复用制造隐藏的包依赖清单；依赖簇围绕相关工作流形成；（3）核心安全结论：仅检查单个技能文档不足，安全相关信号可隐藏在其依赖中——作者沿 ASSC 实际识别并向开发者报告了仍在供应链中存活的已知恶意技能；（4）治理建议：类型化依赖清单、依赖簇一等功能管理、风险警告审计命令、lockfile 式记录。
key_works.how_it_handles_the_example: 对 A→B→C 场景，SDA 的作用是在安装前就把『C 的说明书中引用的临时文件格式与 B 的输出吻合、B 的输入路径与 A 的默认输出一致』这类散落在自然语言里的依赖证据显式化为依赖图。良性开发中这种 A→B→C 链式复用极为常见（依赖簇围绕工作流形成），这解释了为什么 ChainGuard 必须把『候选技能 × 已安装技能』的联合空间作为输入——也说明组合验证的搜索空间随安装基数扩大，是其工程化的主要约束。

background_notes.point: Agent 技能是文件系统级的模块化包（SKILL.md 自然语言指令 + 脚本 + 资源），agent 按需加载；它与工具调用的架构区别在于：工具执行并返回结果，而技能注入程序性知识、修改执行上下文。该标准 2025 年底推出后数月内被 Claude Code、Cursor、GitHub Copilot、Gemini CLI 等采用，单一市场技能数迅速突破 4 万乃至百万量级。
生态风险已有多次实证：3,984 个社区技能审计中 13.4% 携带严重安全问题；综述报告 26.1% 社区技能含漏洞；ClawHavoc 供应链活动在单一市场植入 300+（另一处统计 1,184）个恶意技能，且发生在有官方审查的情况下。

单技能攻击谱系已较成熟：SkillJect（工件通道藏载荷 + 指令通道前置诱导 + 闭环多智能体迭代）、Skill-Inject（基准化测量）、Sleeper（持久状态唤醒）属无触发器常开型；BadSkill 需在技能中捆绑微调模型、SkillTrojan 把加密载荷分片到多个技能并按触发器重组（EHR SQL 上 97.2% ASR / 89.3% 清洁 ACC），属有触发器但高成本型。ElasticBack 的定位正是填补『有条件、低成本、单技能』这一空格。
技能安全的首个系统性威胁建模（生命周期四阶段：创建/分发/部署/执行；七类威胁十七场景）指出：最严重的威胁源于框架本身的结构属性——数据与指令无边界、单次批准即持久信任、市场安全审查非强制——这些无法靠增量修补解决。
声明与实现的偏离是普遍现象：对 49,943 个 OpenClaw 技能的行为完整性验证（BIV，29 能力类型化分类法）发现 80.0% 的技能实际行为偏离声明，其中 81.1% 源于开发者疏忽、18.9% 源于对抗意图，5.0% 携带预测的多阶段攻击链；BIV 在 906 技能恶意检测基准上 F1 达 0.946。
运行时动态审计的独立证据：Runtime Skill Audit (RSA) 通过风险接口画像 + 定向运行时探针 + 沙箱执行，在 100 技能上达 90.0% 准确率（TPR 88%/FPR 8%），比最佳静态基线高 13 个百分点；在自适应自进化攻击下静态检测器 1–2 轮后崩溃，RSA 每轮稳定检出 19–20/20。

权限治理方向：SkillGuard 将技能视为权限承载可执行工件，用双平面模型（上下文影响 + 动作副作用）通过清单、运行时权限控制与策略执行治理；在 SkillInject 数据集上将上下文注入 ASR 从 35.3% 降至 20.7%、明显注入从 36.7% 降至 18.0%。SkillMutator 则显示语言-代码跨模态攻击下开源扫描器仅检出 2%–8%、商业扫描器 9%–17%，其四阶段推理蒸馏扫描器可提升至 88.2%。

open_questions: 组合分析的可扩展性与残余风险：ChainGuard 将 ASR 从 96.0% 压到 22.5%，但残余约两成链仍可通过，且其输入是『候选技能 × 全部已安装技能』的联合空间——在 143 万技能、依赖簇围绕工作流密集形成的生态中（Skills Are Not Islands 的实证），联合分析的计算成本与误报控制如何随安装基数扩展，论文未给出上限分析（来源：ev_a948aa17fb2d, ev_ebdf8657b603）。

条件触发与组合攻击的正交性尚未被统一建模：ElasticBack 证明单技能内的触发器-规则耦合即可绕过部署时防御，ChainGuard 类组合扫描对其天然失明；反过来，纯运行时 taint 方案（SkillDetonate）对休眠载荷需要恰好触发条件命中的探针输入——两类防御各自的覆盖缺口如何互补成一个统一验证框架，目前没有任何工作给出（来源：ev_03467c62cfe6, ev_e4da4cba918a）。

运行时验证的探针覆盖与生态成本：SkillVetBench 显示 89% 的恶意技能威胁来自跨组件交互、RSA 显示运行时审计优于静态，但沙箱执行只能覆盖被探针激活的行为路径；同时 SkillVetBench 发现攻击集中于 exec/write_file/install_skill/spawn 少数高权限原语——『收窄高权限原语的默认授权』与『扩大运行时探针覆盖』哪条路线能以更低的生态摩擦获得更大风险削减，仍是开放的工程争论（来源：ev_4c563aea9279, ev_ae34d6149e7d）。
dossier.narrative_angle: 本期应让读者带走的更新后世界模型：技能安全的盲区不是『扫描器不够聪明』，而是分析单元与攻击单元的结构性错配——扫描器检查的是静态工件（一个个技能），而恶意语义被攻击者存放在了组合空间（ColluSkill：技能间的依赖、工件流、执行交接，96% ASR）和时间条件里（ElasticBack：规则与触发短语的共现，单技能即可）。因此暂定 thesis 需要收窄：组合级验证（ChainGuard 式）确实把盲区从 96% 压缩到 22.5%，是必要的第一层，但它对单技能条件后门天然失明，且残余风险不低；Cloak and Detonate 的 90%+ 规避率进一步证明任何纯安装时审计都会被自适应攻击者绕过，而 SkillDetonate 的 97%/2% 与 SkillVetBench 的两阶段数据表明，把验证对象从『技能长什么样』换成『工作流实际做了什么』（OS 边界信息流证据）才是收敛方向。一句话版本：未来的技能安全栈是三层而非一层——安装时的组合感知（ChainGuard/依赖图）、运行时的行为验证（taint/沙箱）、权限面的原语收窄（exec/write_file/spawn 的默认不信任）；只补其中任何一层，攻击者就把恶意语义搬进剩下两层的缝隙里。

mechanism_cards.problem: 现有技能扫描器主要检查单个技能的指令、权限、依赖和代码行为，跨技能组合产生的风险未被充分检查，导致一个实际盲点：多个局部合理的技能单独通过安全扫描，但在代理执行中组合成有害工作流。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：完整的恶意意图；输出：一组相互依赖的子技能（打包为独立技能），它们单独看似无害，组合后实现原始恶意意图。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 技能之间的交互通过三种机制：上下文依赖（后一技能以前一技能的输出为输入）、工件传递（中间文件或数据作为交接载体）、执行交接（控制流在技能间转移）。每个技能的SKILL.md文件存储其指令、权限、依赖和代码。
algorithm_steps: 使用LLM进行链式规划：将完整的恶意意图分解为若干相互依赖的子载荷，规划它们之间的上下文依赖、工件传递和执行顺序，并将每个子载荷打包为一个独立技能。
生成初始技能链后，将每个子技能提交给目标扫描器，获取该技能是否被标记为可疑。
对于被标记的子技能，基于扫描器反馈迭代重写其SKILL.md文件，在保持整个技能链攻击语义的前提下，降低其可疑信号。

子技能通过上下文依赖、工件传递和执行交接实现重组。
ColluSkill 结合 LLM 链式规划和扫描器反馈重写来降低可疑信号。

mechanism_cards.problem: 在LLM-Agent技能供应链中，攻击者希望在单个技能中植入隐蔽的条件后门，使其仅在用户查询包含特定触发短语时激活恶意负载，而对良性输入保持休眠，且无需修改模型权重或使用多技能，从而绕过现有防御。
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：干净的技能文档(Skill.md)和攻击者定义的目标行为(恶意负载)。输出：已植入后门的技能文档(其中嵌入了规则R)和触发短语T。
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 后门状态由技能文档中的规则R和用户查询中的触发T构成。规则R包含基于负载独特门控词的激活条件；触发T是自然语言短语。攻击期间，受害者agent加载技能，当输入查询包含触发T时，规则R被满足，负载执行。良性查询不包含触发，规则R不激活。接口无运行时状态，完全由文本模板和查询匹配实现。
algorithm_steps: 语义锚定规则注入：从目标负载中提取独特门控词，生成规则R，将R嵌入技能文档Skill.md的低显著性插入点（通过注意力引导的显著性图选择），使R在语义上锚定于技能的正常功能，不易被读出恶意。
冻结规则R并构建触发语料库：冻结已注入的规则R，从自然语料库中收集候选触发短语作为遗传搜索的初始种群。
隐形约束遗传搜索进化触发T：对候选触发短语种群进行变异、交叉，利用适应度函数评估每个候选与冻结R的匹配度，适应度函数优化攻击成功率(ASR)、良性误报率(FPR)和触发短语的隐蔽性（流畅性、连贯性、语法性），迭代进化出最优触发短语T。

evidence.claim: ElasticBack植入规则R和触发T，负载仅在两者共现时触发
采用语义锚定规则注入生成规则R，使其不易被检测
冻结R后，通过隐形约束遗传搜索进化触发T，联合优化有效性和隐蔽性
后门无权重、对良性输入休眠，可绕过部署时防御
高攻击成功率、近零误报率、保持清洁准确率，并跨模型迁移

failure_modes: 如果触发短语在良性查询中意外出现，可能误报（尽管优化后FPR近零）；
如果技能文档被基于困惑度或LLM审核的防御检测到规则R，攻击暴露；
跨模型迁移时性能可能下降；
遗传搜索可能陷入局部最优，导致触发T与R匹配不佳。
limits: 攻击要求攻击者能够预测或控制用户查询中触发短语的出现，实际场景中可能受限；
依赖于特定的技能文档结构和插入点选择的有效性；

未说明门控词提取的具体方法（如是否基于TF-IDF等）；

mechanism_cards.problem: Agent skills from public marketplaces can be malicious, and static scanners can be evaded by adaptive transformations. SkillDetonate aims to detect malicious skills by auditing runtime behavior rather than install-time appearance.
mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: Input: a suspicious agent skill package. Output: a malicious/benign verdict based on observed runtime behaviors.
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: Sandbox execution environment that simulates agent execution with the skill. On-demand closure lift mechanism to observe instructions that become visible only during execution. Marker-based taint tracking: sensitive data sources are marked, and taint is propagated across agent context, file operations, process interactions, and network operations. Detection relies on information-flow evidence crossing OS boundaries (e.g., sensitive data written to a file or sent over network).
algorithm_steps: Execute the skill in a controlled sandbox that mimics the agent's execution environment, granting necessary privileges.
During execution, apply on-demand closure lift to capture the actual sequence of instructions (including any unpacked or obfuscated commands) as they materialize.

While instructions execute, perform marker-based taint analysis: mark sensitive data (e.g., credentials, source code) and propagate taint as data moves through agent context, files, processes, and network operations.

Analyze taint flows to detect security violations: if marked sensitive data flows to an OS-boundary sink (e.g., file write, network send) in a way consistent with exfiltration or malicious modification, flag the skill as malicious.

evidence.claim: SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at 2% false-positive rate and 87% on real-world malicious skills.

failure_modes: False positives (2%) may lead to benign skills being rejected.
False negatives (13% on real-world malicious skills) indicate some evasive skills may still bypass detection.
Sandbox environment may not perfectly replicate all agent capabilities, potentially missing context-dependent behaviors.
limits: Evaluation details (dataset size for SkillDetonate) not provided in excerpt.

Detection may be limited by the quality of taint sources, sandbox fidelity, and evasion techniques that avoid triggering suspicious information flows (e.g., exfiltrating data in small chunks over time).

No details on how taint markers are defined and applied to sensitive data sources.
No information on sandbox implementation or overhead.
Unclear how the system distinguishes between legitimate and malicious information flows.
Missing evaluation on adversarially crafted skills designed to evade dynamic analysis.

mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: Input: a skill comprising natural-language specification, executable code, configuration files, and tool interfaces. Output: a verdict (malicious/benign) supported by auditable runtime evidence.
mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: State: skill artifacts (SKILL.md, code, configs); Stage 1 analysis results (flagged list); sandbox state (file system, processes, network); monitored events log (tool calls, arguments, side effects). Interfaces: Stage 1 semantic analyzer writes flagged skills; Stage 2 sandbox reads flagged skills, agent interacts with skills via tool APIs; monitor captures low-level operations (network, file, exec, credentials). Data structures not specified; sandbox monitoring details insufficient.
algorithm_steps: Step 1: For each skill, extract and parse its natural-language instructions, executable code, configuration files, and tool interfaces.

Step 2: Perform semantic and structural analysis across these components to detect suspicious cross-component patterns (e.g., prompt injection, distributed malicious logic). Flag skills that exhibit such patterns.
Step 3: Deploy flagged skills into an instrumented sandbox environment that monitors network access, filesystem operations, command execution, and credential access.

Step 4: Execute the skill under realistic agent contexts (e.g., with typical prompts/tasks) to trigger potential malicious behaviors. Record runtime events, including tool call sequences, arguments, and side effects.

Step 5: Collect auditable execution traces. Determine a malicious verdict if the traces confirm harmful activity (e.g., unauthorized exec, file writes, credential exfiltration, outbound communication).
failure_modes: Stage 1 semantic analysis may produce false negatives if malicious intent is expressed in novel ways not captured by patterns.
Stage 2 sandbox execution may fail to trigger malicious behavior if the execution context does not include the specific adversarial prompts or conditions needed.
The benchmark relies on a specific agent platform (OpenClaw) and may not generalize to other skill formats or ecosystems.
The sandbox monitoring may miss attacks that use covert channels or timing-based exfiltration.
limits: Limited to skills from the OpenClaw ecosystem and ClawHavoc campaign, may not cover all attack vectors in other agent platforms.
Benchmark is for evaluation, not a real-time defense mechanism; it requires instrumented execution which may be impractical for live systems.
The semantic vetting method is not fully specified; its effectiveness may depend on underlying LLM or analysis tool capabilities.
Sandbox monitoring may introduce overhead and may not perfectly replicate real-world agent environments.
gaps: The paper excerpt does not detail the specific algorithms for semantic vetting or the structural analysis used.
The instrumentation and monitoring framework within the sandbox is not described in the provided text.
No mention of how 'suspicious cross-component patterns' are defined or trained.
No information on the scale of the benchmark dataset beyond mentioning 'confirmed malicious skills' and 1,184 from ClawHavoc.

high_mechanism_cards.problem: 现有技能扫描器主要检查单个技能的指令、权限、依赖和代码行为，跨技能组合产生的风险未被充分检查，导致一个实际盲点：多个局部合理的技能单独通过安全扫描，但在代理执行中组合成有害工作流。
high_mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：完整的恶意意图；输出：一组相互依赖的子技能（打包为独立技能），它们单独看似无害，组合后实现原始恶意意图。
high_mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 技能之间的交互通过三种机制：上下文依赖（后一技能以前一技能的输出为输入）、工件传递（中间文件或数据作为交接载体）、执行交接（控制流在技能间转移）。每个技能的SKILL.md文件存储其指令、权限、依赖和代码。
algorithm_steps: 使用LLM进行链式规划：将完整的恶意意图分解为若干相互依赖的子载荷，规划它们之间的上下文依赖、工件传递和执行顺序，并将每个子载荷打包为一个独立技能。
生成初始技能链后，将每个子技能提交给目标扫描器，获取该技能是否被标记为可疑。
对于被标记的子技能，基于扫描器反馈迭代重写其SKILL.md文件，在保持整个技能链攻击语义的前提下，降低其可疑信号。

high_mechanism_cards.problem: 在LLM-Agent技能供应链中，攻击者希望在单个技能中植入隐蔽的条件后门，使其仅在用户查询包含特定触发短语时激活恶意负载，而对良性输入保持休眠，且无需修改模型权重或使用多技能，从而绕过现有防御。
high_mechanism_cards.inputs_outputs: 输入：干净的技能文档(Skill.md)和攻击者定义的目标行为(恶意负载)。输出：已植入后门的技能文档(其中嵌入了规则R)和触发短语T。
high_mechanism_cards.state_or_interface: 后门状态由技能文档中的规则R和用户查询中的触发T构成。规则R包含基于负载独特门控词的激活条件；触发T是自然语言短语。攻击期间，受害者agent加载技能，当输入查询包含触发T时，规则R被满足，负载执行。良性查询不包含触发，规则R不激活。接口无运行时状态，完全由文本模板和查询匹配实现。
algorithm_steps: 语义锚定规则注入：从目标负载中提取独特门控词，生成规则R，将R嵌入技能文档Skill.md的低显著性插入点（通过注意力引导的显著性图选择），使R在语义上锚定于技能的正常功能，不易被读出恶意。
冻结规则R并构建触发语料库：冻结已注入的规则R，从自然语料库中收集候选触发短语作为遗传搜索的初始种群。
隐形约束遗传搜索进化触发T：对候选触发短语种群进行变异、交叉，利用适应度函数评估每个候选与冻结R的匹配度，适应度函数优化攻击成功率(ASR)、良性误报率(FPR)和触发短语的隐蔽性（流畅性、连贯性、语法性），迭代进化出最优触发短语T。

evidence.claim: ElasticBack植入规则R和触发T，负载仅在两者共现时触发
采用语义锚定规则注入生成规则R，使其不易被检测
冻结R后，通过隐形约束遗传搜索进化触发T，联合优化有效性和隐蔽性
后门无权重、对良性输入休眠，可绕过部署时防御
高攻击成功率、近零误报率、保持清洁准确率，并跨模型迁移

failure_modes: 如果触发短语在良性查询中意外出现，可能误报（尽管优化后FPR近零）；
如果技能文档被基于困惑度或LLM审核的防御检测到规则R，攻击暴露；
跨模型迁移时性能可能下降；
遗传搜索可能陷入局部最优，导致触发T与R匹配不佳。
limits: 攻击要求攻击者能够预测或控制用户查询中触发短语的出现，实际场景中可能受限；
依赖于特定的技能文档结构和插入点选择的有效性；
隐蔽性优化可能降低攻击有效性，需要权衡。
gaps: 原文未提供具体的适应度函数公式或遗传算法的详细超参数；
未说明门控词提取的具体方法（如是否基于TF-IDF等）；
注意力引导的显著性图如何生成未详述；
未评估针对更高级防御（如动态沙盒执行）的绕过能力。

evidence.title: ColluSkill: Adversarial Cross-Skill Composition for Evading Agent Skill Scanners
evidence.excerpt: ColluSkill: Adversarial Cross-Skill Composition for Evading Agent Skill Scanners Puyu Zeng 1 , Simeng Qin 2 , Jingzhi Li 3 , Ju Jia 4 , Zheli Liu 1 , Xiaojun Jia 5 \corresponding Abstract Agent skills are emerging as an important attack surface in LLM-based agent systems. Through an empirical study of existing skill scanners, we find that current defenses primarily inspect individual skills, including their instructions, permissions, dependencies, and code behaviors, which can leave risks arising from cross-skill composition insufficiently examined. This creates a practical blind spot: multiple locally plausible skills may independently pass security scanning while collectively forming a harmful workflow during agent execution. To systematically investigate this threat, we propose ColluSkill, a collusive multi-skill-chain attack framework that decomposes a complete malicious intent into several interdependent sub-payloads and embeds them into independently packaged skills. Thus, the attack does not rely on any single malicious skill, but on the ordered composition of locally plausible behaviors through contextual dependencies, artifact passing, and execution handoffs. ColluSkill further employs LLM-based chain planning and scanner-feedback refinement to preserve chain-level attack semantics while iteratively reducing suspicious signals within individual sub-skills. To defend against such attacks, we further propose ChainGuard, a context-aware skill-chain scanner that jointly analyzes a candidate skill and the skills already installed in the agent environment. ChainGuard reconstructs cross-skill dependencies, artifact flows, capability compositions, and potential downstream behaviors to identify risks that emerge only at the workflow level. Extensive experiments on six representative skill scanners show that ColluSkill achieves an average attack success rate of 96.0% and consistently outperforms the evaluated single-skill and multi-skill attack baselines. Meanwhile, ChainGuard reduces the attack success rate to 22.5% while allowing 99.5% of benign workflows to pass, highlighting the importance of chain-level security analysis for agent skill ecosystems. Introduction Agent skills are becoming an important way to extend the capabilities of Large Language Model agents (Wang et al. 2024 , 2023 ; Xi et al. 2025 ; Yao et al. 2022 ; Liu et al. 2025 ; Du et al. 2026 ) . A skill usually combines task instructions, tool interfaces, executable scripts, and external resources into a reusable module, allowing an agent to gain new abilities more easily (Schmotz et al. 2025 ; Liang et al. 2026 ; Zhou et al. 2026 ; Jiang et al. 2026 ) . This modular design improves the reuse and scalability of agent systems and has supported the rapid growth of agent frameworks and skill-sharing platforms (Zheng et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ; Pu et al. 2026 ; Saha and Hemanth 2026 ) . However, the same flexibility also introduces new security risks because a skill may do more than provide text instructions (Jia et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2026 ) . It can execute code, read or write files, call external APIs, and access system resources (Ruan et al. 2024 ) . Once a malicious skill is installed, these capabilities may be abused to leak sensitive data, contact external services, or misuse the permissions available to the agent (Qu et al. 2026 ; Guo et al. 2026a ; Kim et al. 2026 ) . Figure 1: Overview of the cross-skill composition blind spot. Existing scanners primarily inspect individual skills, while runtime composition can recover unsafe chain-level behavior from locally plausible sub-skills. To reduce these risks, a growing ecosystem of skill scanners and checking tools is appearing. Cisco’s Skill Scanner combines rule checking, Large Language Model meaning analysis, and behavior data flow analysis to find known or possible threats in agent skills (Cisco AI Defense 2026 ) . Snyk’s Agent Scan expands security scanning to agent parts, focusing on risks like prompt injection, untrusted content, credential handling, and hardcoded keys (Snyk 2025 ) . Checking tools for skill markets, like Skill Vetter, look at permission limits, suspicious commands, and possible dangerous actions before a skill is installed or used (fedrov 2025 ) . The community is also exploring audit templates that use prompts. For example, ClawGuard provides an "auditor-skill" template to scan agent skills (Ying et al. 2026 ) . (Liu et al. 2026b ) did a large-scale study on skill weaknesses and proposed HSS-Scan, which combines static pattern analysis, meaning checks, and Large Language Model scanning to detect malicious skills. Bhardwaj proposed SkillFortify to analyze security risks in the agent skill chain (Bhardwaj 2026 ) . At the same time, some general code security tools are starting to cover agent skill scenarios. For instance, VirusTotal’s Code Insight can analyze the actual behavior of OpenClaw skills from a security perspective (Quintero 2026 ) . Through an empirical study of existing skill scanners, we find that current defenses mainly inspect individual skills, focusing on their instructions, permissions, dependencies, and code behaviors. Prior attacks such as SkillJect, SkillInject, BadSkill, and Cloak also mainly study malicious behavior within a single skill (Jia et al. 2026a ; Schmotz et al. 2026 ; Tie et al. 2026 ; Ji et al. 2026 ) . Recent work has formalized security risks arising from multi-skill composition and evaluated them through controlled benchmark settings (Xie et al. 2026 ) . However, the robustness of current skill scanners against collusive skill chains constructed through LLM-based chain planning and iteratively refined using scanner feedback has not been systematically studied, leaving a practical blind spot in existing defenses. In real agent environments, multiple skills can be installed, invoked, and combined into a continuous workflow (Li et al. 2026a ) . An attacker can therefore spread a complete malicious intent across several interdependent skills, allowing each skill to appear normal or low-risk on its own while the full attack behavior emerges through their ordered composition during agent execution. To study this problem, we propose ColluSkill, a collusive multi-skill-chain attack framework against agent skill scanners. ColluSkill draws on Norbert Elias’s concept of interdependence chains (Elias 1978 ) as a conceptual lens for explaining how local roles can jointly produce chain-level behavior through dependency and order. Based on this view, ColluSkill decomposes a complete malicious intent into several interdependent sub-payloads and maps them to independently packaged sub-skills. Their contextual dependencies, artifact passing, and execution handoffs preserve the complete chain-level attack semantics. ColluSkill goes beyond simple multi-skill composition by combining LLM-based chain planning with scanner-feedback refinement. A direct payload split often produces separate, independent pieces rather than an interdependent skill chain. ColluSkill therefore plans the contextual dependencies, artifact passing, and execution order among sub-skills. After generating the initial skill chain, it submits each sub-skill to the target scanners and iteratively rewrites the flagged sub-skills based on scanner feedback. This process reduces suspicious signals in flagged sub-skills while preserving the chain-level attack semantics of the full workflow. To reduce this risk, we further propose ChainGuard, a context-aware skill-chain scanner. Unlike traditional scanners that inspect skills in isolation, ChainGuard analyzes a candidate skill together with all skills already installed in the current environment. It is not given the true attack-chain membership and must identify possible cross-skill relations from the installed-skill context. This allows ChainGuard to detect risky behaviors that only appear when multiple skills work together in practice. We systematically evaluate ColluSkill on six representative skill scanners and compare it with existing single-skill and multi-skill attack baselines. The results show that ColluSkill achieves an average ASR of 96.0% and the best attack performance among the evaluated methods. Further ablation experiments show that the effectiveness of ColluSkill does not come from simple payload splitting. Chain planning increases the average ASR from 36.7% to 68.2%, and scanner-feedback refinement further raises it to 96.0%. Runtime experiments also show that ColluSkill attack chains can successfully execute on OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex across different model backbones, showing that adversarial cross-skill composition can lead to effective attacks during real agent execution. We further evaluate ChainGuard against this threat and find that it reduces the ASR of ColluSkill to 22.5% while allowing 99.5% of benign workflows to pass. In summary, the main contributions are in three aspects: 1. We propose ColluSkill, a collusive multi-skill-chain attack that spreads malicious intent across multiple sub-skills and uses chain planning and scanner-feedback refinement to preserve the full attack behavior while reducing local suspicious signals. 2. We propose ChainGuard, a context-aware skill-chain scanner that detects cross-skill composition risks by analyzing a candidate skill together with all installed skills. 3. We conduct systematic experiments on six skill scanners and three coding agents. ColluSkill achieves an average ASR of 96.0% and the best attack performance, while ChainGuard reduces the ASR to 22.5% and allows 99.5% of benign workflows to pass. Related Work Agent Skills and Their Security Risks Agent skills have recently become an important way to extend LLM agents with reusable task abilities (Ling et al. 2026 ; Xu and Yan 2026 ; Jia et al. 2026b ) . Prior work views skills as modular units for ability reuse, and Anthropic further standardizes a skill as a SKILL.md-based folder that can include scripts and resources and be loaded by the agent when needed (Li et al. 2026b ; Li 2026 ) . With systems such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode supporting skills, and sharing platforms such as OpenClaw and ClawHub growing, skills are becoming an installable and shareable agent extension ecosystem. At the same time, recent studies show that this ecosystem introduces new security risks (Li et al. 2026c ) . Liu et al. analyzed 31,132 public skills from 42,447 collected skills and found that 26.1% contain at least one vulnerability, including prompt injection, data leaks, privilege escalation, and supply chain risks (Liu et al. 2026b ) . Schmotz et al. proposed Skill-Inject and showed that skill files can serve as an effective prompt-injection channel, leading to data leaks, destructive actions, and high attack success rates in real agent environments (Schmotz et al. 2026 ) . Jia et al. further proposed SkillJect, which uses closed-loop optimization to generate hidden and triggerable malicious skills for coding agents (Jia et al. 2026a ) . A separate large-scale study also confirmed that verifiable malicious skills already exist in real skill repositories (Liu et al. 2026a ; Beurer-Kellner et al. 2026 ) . Overall, these works show that agent skills are not only a mechanism for ability extension, but also a real and growing attack surface. Skill scanners. evidence.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger–Rule Optimization
evidence.excerpt: ElasticBack : Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger–Rule Optimization Hao Sui 1 , Simeng Qin 2 , Jie Liao 3 , Xiaojun Jia 4 \corresponding , Bing Chen 1 \corresponding , Yang Liu 4 Abstract Agent skills, bundles of instructions and resources that an LLM agent loads on demand, form an emerging supply chain where a single poisoned skill can persistently compromise every agent that installs it. However, existing skill attacks either fire on every request or rely on fine-tuned weights or multiple skills, leaving a conditional and low-cost backdoor unexplored. In this work, we present ElasticBack , an effective conditional single-skill backdoor that plants a rule R R in the skill document and a benign-looking trigger T T in the user query, so the malicious payload fires only when both co-occur. ElasticBack binds the two sides through a trigger-as-switch construction, generating R R via semantic-anchored rule injection. It then freezes R R and evolves T T against it with a stealth-constrained genetic search, so that effectiveness and stealth are optimized, keeping the backdoor weight-free and dormant on benign inputs. Extensive experiments across three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show that ElasticBack attains a high attack success rate at a near-zero false-positive rate with preserved clean accuracy, transfers across models, and evades deployment-time defenses. These results motivate stronger defenses for the skill supply chain. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents (Yehudai et al. 2026 ; Ma et al. 2026 ) are now widely applied across coding (Islam et al. 2024 ) , data analysis (Hong et al. 2025 ) , and customer support (Zhang et al. 2025b ) , where they go beyond generating text to autonomously execute actions on the user’s behalf. To gain new capabilities more conveniently, they can load skills without retraining (Zhou et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2026a ) : a skill is a reusable bundle of a natural-language instruction file ( Skill.md ) and supporting resources such as scripts, templates, or data, invoked whenever a task matches its domain. Today, skills have become an indispensable part of modern agent systems (Ling et al. 2026 ) . Yet the convenience and practicality that make skills so widely used also turn them into a dangerous attack surface (Xu and Yan 2026 ; Jia et al. 2026b ) , since a single poisoned skill can persistently harm every user who installs it. Therefore, the security threats facing agent skills demand urgent and systematic study. The risk is already confirmed by an audit of 3,984 community skills, 13.4% of which carry severe security issues (Liu et al. 2026 ) . Agent-skill security has drawn growing attention (Badhe and Tiwari 2026 ; Li et al. 2026d ) , and existing attacks fall into two forms. The first fires indiscriminately, with no attacker-controlled trigger. SkillJect (Jia et al. 2026a ) and Skill-Inject (Qu et al. 2026 ) embed always-on malicious instructions in Skill.md , while Sleeper attacks (Li et al. 2026c ) wake from a persistent state on ordinary benign queries. The second fires under an attacker-controlled trigger but at higher cost. BadSkill (Tie et al. 2026 ) needs a fine-tuned model bundled in the skill, and SkillTrojan (Feng et al. 2026 ) shards an encrypted payload across multiple skills. However, prior attacks fire without an attacker-controlled trigger or depend on fine-tuned weights or multiple skills, making it difficult to implement stealthy, low-cost skill backdoors (Fig. 1 (b)). Figure 1: The pipeline of the skill backdoor attack in LLM agents and the gap in prior attacks. Motivation. In real-world scenarios, an attacker who deploys a stealthy, low-cost backdoor skill can cause severe harm. Because such a skill backdoor is weight-free and runs only when triggered, it is hard to detect and easy to spread. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), the backdoor consists of a rule hidden inside the skill and a benign-looking trigger phrase in the query. It stays silent, passes review on ordinary requests, and fires its payload only when the trigger appears. Current defenses inspect a skill only at rest or on benign queries, so this dormant rule slips through undetected. Therefore, it is urgent to develop stealthy and low-cost conditional backdoor attacks tailored for LLM-agent skills to advance the development of more robust defense mechanisms. To achieve this, we present ElasticBack , an effective framework for planting a stealthy, low-cost conditional backdoor in agent skills. Since an installed skill is trusted, ElasticBack embeds a conditional rule R R in Skill.md and the trigger T T in the user query, firing the payload only when both co-occur. This raises two main challenges: ❶ How to separately generate R R and T T so that the payload fires reliably under the trigger yet stays dormant on benign queries? ❷ How to keep both R R and T T stealthy enough to evade perplexity screening and LLM-judge auditing? Firstly, since R R and T T are generated separately and the adversary cannot see the victim’s runtime queries, a naively chosen rule and trigger tend to misalign. A loosely worded rule matches benign requests and misfires, while a generic trigger fails to satisfy the rule reliably. Thus, the key challenge is to bind a separately generated rule and trigger so that the payload fires precisely under the trigger and never otherwise . To this end, ElasticBack adopts a trigger-as-switch design. A small set of payload-derived gate words bridges the two sides, seeding the rule’s activation condition and anchoring the evolution of the trigger, so the trigger becomes the sole switch that flips the payload on. Then, a guided search aligns T T against a frozen R R , so the rule and trigger stay consistent by construction and ASR \mathrm{ASR} and FPR \mathrm{FPR} can be driven separately. Secondly, both R R in Skill.md and T T in the query are exposed to detectors. A rule inserted at an arbitrary position or written freely stands out, whether by a perplexity spike or by an LLM judge that flags the out-of-place instruction. Meanwhile, a conspicuous or ungrammatical trigger is caught by perplexity screening. Thus, another key challenge is to make both the rule and the trigger read as natural parts of their host text while preserving the attack . To tackle this, ElasticBack hides R R at a low-salience insertion point from an attention-guided saliency map and folds fluency, coherence, and grammaticality into the search objective. Stealth is optimized jointly with effectiveness, not as an afterthought, keeping both sides inconspicuous without sacrificing attack success. In summary, the contributions of our paper are: • To the best of our knowledge, we devise the first conditional single-skill backdoor attack, named ElasticBack , which is capable of executing malicious tasks under the attacker-controlled trigger without affecting normal tasks. • We propose a semantic-anchored rule injection approach that generates a gated rule R R from payload-unique gate words. On this basis, we further design a corpus-driven trigger evolution method that evolves the trigger T T against the frozen R R via a stealth-constrained genetic search, jointly optimizing effectiveness and dual-side stealth. • We conduct extensive experiments across three target behaviors, each evaluated on 50 skills, and four agent LLMs against recent skill attacks and deployment-time defenses. Experimental results show that ElasticBack attains high ASR \mathrm{ASR} at near-zero FPR \mathrm{FPR} with preserved CAC \mathrm{CAC} . 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 LLM Agents and Agent Skills An LLM agent (Duan et al. 2025 ; Yehudai et al. 2026 ) augments a language-model backbone with a harness that lets it reason over a task, call external tools, and run code on the user’s behalf. Modern agent frameworks such as Claude Code (Anthropic 2025a ) , Codex CLI (OpenAI 2025 ) , and Gemini CLI (Google 2025 ) load skills on demand, since no fixed prompt covers tasks across all domains. Anthropic (Anthropic 2025b ) formalizes this pattern as the open agent skills specification, in which a skill bundles an instruction file ( Skill.md ) with optional scripts, templates, or data. Guided only by a short description , the agent judges whether a skill fits the current task and, on a match, it reads the full Skill.md and executes its instructions. Because such skills are openly published and adopted almost verbatim (Liu et al. 2026 ) , each becomes an artifact the agent implicitly trusts rather than untrusted data it screens. Therefore, tampering with a single published skill can silently redirect every agent that adopts it, without any access to model weights. 2.2 Backdoor Attacks and Defenses on Agent Systems Classical backdoor attacks poison training data or model parameters so that a trigger produces an attacker-chosen output while clean inputs behave normally. They have been studied on images (Liu et al. 2024b ; Xun et al. 2024 ; Shen et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025a ) , graphs (Sui et al. 2026b , a ) , and recently LLMs (Li et al. 2026b ; Yan et al. 2026 ) . None achieves a weight-free and conditional skill backdoor attack in agent systems. These catch overt payloads but miss a dormant conditional rule. Therefore, we instantiate three such detectors as baselines in § 5 . evidence.title: SkCC: Portable and Secure Skill Compilation for Cross-Framework LLM Agents
evidence.excerpt: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills (e.g., SKILL markdown files) to execute complex tasks, yet these artifacts lack portability: agent frameworks are highly sensitive to prompt formatting, leading to a large performance variation for the same skill. Nevertheless, most skills are authored once as format-agnostic Markdown, necessitating costly per-framework rewrites and also leaving security largely unaddressed, with widespread vulnerabilities in practice. To address this, we present SkCC, a compiler for LLM agents that introduces classical compilation design into agent skill development. SkCC centers on SkIR, a strongly-typed intermediate representation that decouples skill semantics from framework-specific formatting, thus enabling portable deployment across agent frameworks. Atop of this IR, a static Optimizer enforces security constraints, blocking vulnerabilities before deployment. Implemented as a four-phase pipeline, SkCC effectively reduces adaptation complexity from $O(m \times n)$ to $O(m + n)$ across $m$ skills and $n$ frameworks. Experiments on SkillsBench demonstrate that SkCC delivers consistent and substantial gains over original counterparts, with pass rate increases from 21.1% to 33.3% on Claude Code and from 35.1% to 48.7% on Kimi CLI. Further, the design achieves sub-10ms compilation latency, 94.8% proactive security trigger rate, and 10-46% runtime token savings across frameworks.

evidence.title: Toward User Comprehension Supports for LLM Agent Skill Specifications
evidence.excerpt: Users often interpret and select agent skills through their SKILL markdown specifications. To protect users, existing audits mainly focus on malicious or unsafe skills. We study the complementary question of whether specifications help users form bounded expectations about what a skill consumes, produces, and covers. Across 878 cybersecurity skills, we used rule-based coding to measure textual cues for four comprehension anchors, namely operational basis, output contract, boundary disclosure, and example capability demonstration. Cues for operational basis were common, but only 19.0% of specifications exhibited cues for an example task, sample, or expected outcome, and only 2.3% exhibited cues for all four anchors. We further examined a small DNS/C2 telemetry subset (n$=$6) to illustrate why missing examples may matter. Examples appeared to make first local checks easier to construct, while no-example skills typically required helper code inspection to recover command arguments or output fields. We argue that agent-skill evaluation should treat specifications as user-facing capability disclosures, not merely as containers for executable instructions.

evidence.title: Skill-as-Pseudocode: Refactoring Skill Libraries to Pseudocode for LLM Agents
evidence.excerpt: Markdown skill libraries for LLM agents ship as free-form prose, forcing the agent to re-derive both the input schema and the concrete invocation syntax on every retrieval. We observe that this often produces a "confused -> re-retrieve -> still confused" loop in which the agent issues a partially-correct action, receives uninformative environment feedback, and re-retrieves the same prose. We propose Skill-as-Pseudocode (SaP), an automatic conversion of markdown skill libraries into typed pseudocode with deterministic quality control. For each cluster of similar procedural passages drawn from one or more skills, SaP extracts a typed contract and filters it through a four-check deterministic verifier (coverage, binding, replacement, risk). Promoted contracts are inlined into a rewritten skill skeleton together with restored concrete action templates, giving the agent two complementary signals: a typed signature for what the skill does and a concrete template for how to invoke it. On the 134-game ALFWorld unseen split with gpt-4o-mini, pooled across three seeds, SaP wins 82/402 paired games versus 47/402 for the Graph-of-Skills (GoS) baseline (pooled McNemar p = 8.2e-5), at -22.8 +/- 6.4% input tokens and -14.5 +/- 4.1% LLM calls per game.

evidence.title: ColluSkill: Adversarial Cross-Skill Composition for Evading Agent Skill Scanners
evidence.excerpt: Agent skills are emerging as an important attack surface in LLM-based agent systems. Through an empirical study of existing skill scanners, we find that current defenses mainly inspect individual skills, leaving risks from cross-skill composition insufficiently examined. This creates a practical blind spot: multiple locally plausible skills may pass security checks while collectively forming a harmful workflow during agent execution. To investigate this threat, we propose ColluSkill, a collusive multi-skill-chain attack framework that decomposes a complete malicious intent into interdependent sub-payloads embedded in independently packaged skills. The attack does not rely on any single malicious skill, but emerges from the ordered composition of locally plausible behaviors through contextual dependencies, artifact passing, and execution handoffs. ColluSkill further employs LLM-based chain planning and scanner-feedback refinement to preserve chain-level attack semantics while reducing suspicious signals in individual sub-skills. To defend against such attacks, we propose ChainGuard, a context-aware skill-chain scanner that jointly analyzes a candidate skill and the skills already installed in the agent environment. ChainGuard reconstructs cross-skill dependencies, artifact flows, capability compositions, and downstream behaviors to identify risks that emerge only at the workflow level. Experiments on six representative skill scanners show that ColluSkill achieves an average attack success rate of 96.0% and consistently outperforms the evaluated single-skill and multi-skill attack baselines. Meanwhile, ChainGuard reduces the attack success rate to 22.5% while allowing 99.5% of benign workflows to pass, highlighting the importance of chain-level security analysis for agent skill ecosystems.

evidence.title: ACE: A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems
evidence.excerpt: LLM-integrated app systems extend the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) with third-party apps that are invoked by a system LLM using interleaved planning and execution phases to answer user queries. These systems introduce new attack vectors where malicious apps can cause integrity violation of planning or execution, availability breakdown, or privacy compromise during execution. In this work, we identify new attacks impacting the integrity of planning, as well as the integrity and availability of execution in LLM-integrated apps, and demonstrate them against IsolateGPT, a recent solution designed to mitigate attacks from malicious apps. We propose Abstract-Concrete-Execute (ACE), a new secure architecture for LLM-integrated app systems that provides security guarantees for system planning and execution. Specifically, ACE decouples planning into two phases by first creating an abstract execution plan using only trusted information, and then mapping the abstract plan to a concrete plan using installed system apps. We verify that the plans generated by our system satisfy user-specified secure information flow constraints via static analysis on the structured plan output. During execution, ACE enforces data and capability barriers between apps, and ensures that the execution is conducted according to the trusted abstract plan. We show experimentally that ACE is secure against attacks from the InjecAgent and Agent Security Bench benchmarks for indirect prompt injection, and our newly introduced attacks. We also evaluate the utility of ACE in realistic environments, using the Tool Usage suite from the LangChain benchmark. Our architecture represents a significant advancement towards hardening LLM-based systems using system security principles.

evidence.title: Agent Skills for Large Language Models: Architecture, Acquisition, Security, and the Path Forward
evidence.excerpt: The transition from monolithic language models to modular, skill-equipped agents marks a defining shift in how large language models (LLMs) are deployed in practice. Rather than encoding all procedural knowledge within model weights, agent skills -- composable packages of instructions, code, and resources that agents load on demand -- enable dynamic capability extension without retraining. It is formalized in a paradigm of progressive disclosure, portable skill definitions, and integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This survey provides a comprehensive treatment of the agent skills landscape, as it has rapidly evolved during the last few months. We organize the field along four axes: (i) architectural foundations, examining the SKILL$.$md specification, progressive context loading, and the complementary roles of skills and MCP; (ii) skill acquisition, covering reinforcement learning with skill libraries, autonomous skill discovery (SEAgent), and compositional skill synthesis; (iii) deployment at scale, including the computer-use agent (CUA) stack, GUI grounding advances, and benchmark progress on OSWorld and SWE-bench; and (iv) security, where recent empirical analyses reveal that 26.1% of community-contributed skills contain vulnerabilities, motivating our proposed Skill Trust and Lifecycle Governance Framework -- a four-tier, gate-based permission model that maps skill provenance to graduated deployment capabilities. We identify seven open challenges -- from cross-platform skill portability to capability-based permission models -- and propose a research agenda for realizing trustworthy, self-improving skill ecosystems. Unlike prior surveys that broadly cover LLM agents or tool use, this work focuses specifically on the emerging skill abstraction layer and its implications for the next generation of agentic systems. Project repo: https://github.com/scienceaix/agentskills

evidence.title: Focus Agent: LLM-Powered Virtual Focus Group
evidence.excerpt: In the domain of Human-Computer Interaction, focus groups represent a widely utilised yet resource-intensive methodology, often demanding the expertise of skilled moderators and meticulous preparatory efforts. This study introduces the ``Focus Agent,'' a Large Language Model (LLM) powered framework that simulates both the focus group (for data collection) and acts as a moderator in a focus group setting with human participants. To assess the data quality derived from the Focus Agent, we ran five focus group sessions with a total of 23 human participants as well as deploying the Focus Agent to simulate these discussions with AI participants. Quantitative analysis indicates that Focus Agent can generate opinions similar to those of human participants. Furthermore, the research exposes some improvements associated with LLMs acting as moderators in focus group discussions that include human participants.

evidence.title: Agentic Skill Discovery
evidence.excerpt: Language-conditioned robotic skills make it possible to apply the high-level reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) to low-level robotic control. A remaining challenge is to acquire a diverse set of fundamental skills. Existing approaches either manually decompose a complex task into atomic robotic actions in a top-down fashion, or bootstrap as many combinations as possible in a bottom-up fashion to cover a wider range of task possibilities. These decompositions or combinations, however, require an initial skill library. For example, a ``grasping'' capability can never emerge from a skill library containing only diverse ``pushing'' skills. Existing skill discovery techniques with reinforcement learning acquire skills by an exhaustive exploration but often yield non-meaningful behaviors. In this study, we introduce a novel framework for skill discovery that is entirely driven by LLMs. The framework begins with an LLM generating task proposals based on the provided scene description and the robot's configurations, aiming to incrementally acquire new skills upon task completion. For each proposed task, a series of reinforcement learning processes are initiated, utilizing reward and success determination functions sampled by the LLM to develop the corresponding policy. The reliability and trustworthiness of learned behaviors are further ensured by an independent vision-language model. We show that starting with zero skill, the skill library emerges and expands to more and more meaningful and reliable skills, enabling the robot to efficiently further propose and complete advanced tasks. Project page: \url{https://agentic-skill-discovery.github.io}.

evidence.title: Skill-SD: Skill-Conditioned Self-Distillation for Multi-turn LLM Agents
evidence.excerpt: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely used to train LLM agents for multi-turn interactive tasks, but its sample efficiency is severely limited by sparse rewards and long horizons. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) alleviates this by providing dense token-level supervision from a privileged teacher that has access to ground-truth answers. However, such fixed privileged information cannot capture the diverse valid strategies in agent tasks, and naively combining OPSD with RL often leads to training collapse. To address these limitations, we introduce Skill-SD, a framework that turns the agent's own trajectories into dynamic training-only supervision. Completed trajectories are summarized into compact natural language skills that describe successful behaviors, mistakes, and workflows. These skills serve as dynamic privileged information conditioning only the teacher, while the student always acts under the plain task prompt and learns to internalize the guidance through distillation. To stabilize the training, we derive an importance-weighted reverse-KL loss to provide gradient-correct token-level distillation, and dynamically synchronize the teacher with the improving student. Experimental results on agentic benchmarks demonstrate that Skill-SD substantially outperforms the standard RL baseline, improving both vanilla GRPO (+14.0%/+10.9% on AppWorld/Sokoban) and vanilla OPD (+42.1%/+40.6%). Project page: https://k1xe.github.io/skill-sd/

evidence.title: Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
evidence.excerpt: LLM coding agents increasingly rely on third-party agent skills from public marketplaces, which execute with the agent's privileges and create a software supply-chain attack surface: a malicious skill can steal credentials, exfiltrate source code, or install backdoors. Existing defenses use static skill scanners based on pattern matching or LLM-as-judge analysis, but it remains unclear whether they withstand adaptive evasions that preserve malicious behavior while changing payload appearance. This paper first presents an adversarial study of existing skill scanners through SkillCloak, a payload-preserving evasion framework that keeps the attack semantics intact while transforming their visible form. SkillCloak uses two complementary strategies: Structural Obfuscation, which rewrites visible payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms, and Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing, which hides malicious components from the install-time view and restores them during agent execution. Across eight scanners and 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills, SFS Packing bypasses every scanner at over 90%, while Structural Obfuscation bypasses over 80% on most static scanners and reaches 96% on a hybrid scanner, showing that appearance-based auditing is insufficient. Motivated by this finding, we propose SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor that executes skills in a sandbox and detects malicious effects through OS-boundary information-flow evidence rather than install-time appearance. SkillDetonate combines on-demand closure lift, which observes instructions materialized during execution, with marker-based taint analysis, which tracks sensitive-data flows across the agent context, files, processes, and network operations. The results show that SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at a 2% false-positive rate and sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.

The results show that SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at a 2% false-positive rate and sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills. I Introduction LLM agents are rapidly moving from demonstrations to real-world deployment across domains, including software engineering (e.g., “vibe coding” assistants [ 28 ] ), cybersecurity [ 67 ] , and autonomous driving [ 38 ] . A key enabler of this transition is the emergence of Agent Skills : modular packages that allow agents such as Claude Code [ 4 ] and OpenAI Codex [ 44 ] to acquire new capabilities on demand. A skill is typically distributed as a structured directory containing natural-language instructions (e.g., SKILL.md ), executable scripts or code blocks, and auxiliary resources that an agent can load and invoke during task execution [ 3 ] . Because skills are model-agnostic, composable, and shareable as ordinary files, they are increasingly becoming a unit of capability distribution for agentic systems, with public skill marketplaces growing rapidly [ 3 , 39 ] . The scale of this ecosystem is already substantial: within months of the open standard being introduced in late 2025, a single marketplace had accumulated over 40,000 publicly listed skills [ 35 ] , the overwhelming majority of which are community-contributed and unvetted. This extensibility, however, introduces a new software supply-chain risk. Once installed, a skill is interpreted and executed by an agent that may have access to the developer’s workspace, local files, credentials, package managers, terminals, and external services. A malicious skill can therefore abuse these inherited privileges to perform security-sensitive actions, including credential theft, source-code exfiltration, backdoor installation, and destructive file operations. For instance, the recent ClawHavoc campaign planted over 300 malicious skills on a single public marketplace, whose SKILL.md files instructed the agent to fetch and run an information stealer under the guise of an installation prerequisite, silently harvesting the victim’s browser credentials, keychain passwords, SSH keys, and cryptocurrency wallets [ 31 ] . The attack surface is particularly broad, and the malicious payload can be embedded in the natural-language instructions of SKILL.md , or hidden in bundled scripts or resources. A range of malicious behaviors have already been observed in published skills, including credential theft [ 7 , 31 ] , data exfiltration [ 58 , 37 ] , and backdoor deployment [ 36 ] . Problem. To mitigate these risks, recent efforts have proposed skill scanners that audit third-party skills before installation [ 23 , 60 , 63 ] . They are designed to recognize suspicious patterns in the skill’s visible files, using static rules, LLM-based judgments, or their combination. However, it remains unclear whether such static auditing mechanisms can withstand adaptive evasion. An adversarial skill author is not constrained to expose the malicious payload in the form expected by the scanner; the payload can be rewritten, relocated, or or staging the payload until runtime. This raises a fundamental question: To what extent can current skill auditing mechanisms detect malicious skills under semantics-preserving evasive transformations? Figure 1 : Overview of SkillCloak and SkillDetonate . As Figure ˜ 1 illustrates, static scanners flag a malicious skill, but SkillCloak rewrites it into a variant they clear as safe , whereas SkillDetonate detects both the original and cloaked skills by auditing their runtime behavior. Adversarial Study. To address this problem, we first conduct an adversarial study on eight representative skill scanners and two production agents (Codex and Claude Code) with 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills. We propose SkillCloak , a payload-preserving evasion framework that adaptively transforms malicious skills while preserving their malicious behavior. SkillCloak operates on two complementary strategies (Section III ). 1. Structural Obfuscation rewrites concrete payload indicators (e.g., malicious instructions, shell commands, URLs, and credential-related strings) into semantically equivalent forms that evade static rules and LLM-based judgments. This strategy perturbs the skill’s structure minimally, making it stealthy with strong bypass effectiveness. 2. Self-Extracting Skill Packing (SFS Packing) hides malicious instructions or scripts outside the scanner’s observable scope (e.g., ignored directories or encoded resource blobs) and restores them at execution time. This strategy alters the skill’s structure substantially, but achieves near-complete bypass effectiveness. We collected 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills from the ClawHub skills archive [ 45 ] , and employ SkillCloak to generate evasion skills for adversarial evaluation. The results show that 1. existing skill scanners are highly vulnerable to semantics-preserving evasions: with SFS Packing , over 90 % 90\% of evasion skills bypass all scanners, while Structural Obfuscation bypasses over 80 % 80\% on most static scanners and up to 96 % 96\% on a hybrid scanner. 2. SkillCloak generates payload-preserving evasion skills that stay functional: across both Codex and Claude Code, cloaking causes no statistically detectable loss in skill utility. These findings show the limits of existing static skill auditing against evasive malware and motivate the need of behavior-centric defense . Behavior-Centric Auditor. To meet this need, we propose SkillDetonate , a behavior-centric runtime auditor for agent skills. The key insight is that evasion can alter how a payload is written, packaged, or staged, but they must produce observable behaviors and effects to achieve a malicious objective. SkillDetonate therefore executes a suspicious skill in a controlled sandbox and monitors the security-relevant effects it produces during agent execution. To achieve this, SkillDetonate introduces two novel designs. 1. On-Demand Closure Lift captures and executes the natural-language instructions a skill materializes at runtime, feeding them back into the agent’s session. This mitigates the path-coverage gaps typically exploited by multi-stage malware. 2. Marker-Based Taint Analysis tracks information flow across the two media a syscall monitor cannot natively follow. Data markers, planted at sensitive reads intercepted through a FUSE virtual filesystem, carry provenance through the agent’s natural-language context; and inode-level reconstruction of the eBPF syscall graph recovers that same flow across opaque cross-process byte transforms. We evaluated SkillDetonate on SkillJect [ 27 ] , a benchmark of 150 150 malicious skills that inject prompt-injection payloads into skill-enabled agents. The results show that SkillDetonate can successfully detect 97 % 97\% of malicious skills at a 2 % 2\% false-positive rate, 31 % 31\% more than the best static scanner and 62 % 62\% more than a naive OpenCode based agent detector. On real-world malicious skills from MalSkillBench [ 19 ] , SkillDetonate sustains 87 % 87\% detection and stays stable under SkillCloak , whereas the best static scanner collapses from 99 % 99\% to 10 % 10\% under Structural Obfuscation. In this paper, we make the following contributions. • To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to evaluate existing skill auditing mechanisms against adaptive semantics-preserving evasion . The results show that existing auditing mechanisms are highly vulnerable to semantics-preserving evasions. • We propose SkillCloak , a skill evasion framework to transforms malicious skills while preserving the payload via two complementary strategy ( Structural Obfuscation and Self-Extracting Skill Packing ). • We propose SkillDetonate , a behavior-centric runtime auditor for agent skills to detect malicious skills by observing security-relevant effects during agent execution with two novel designs ( On-Demand Closure Lift and Marker-Based Taint Analysis ). • We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of SkillDetonate . II Background and Goal II-A Malicious Agent Skills. An agent skill is a structured directory bundle containing natural-language instructions, executable components, and auxiliary resources that a host agent discovers by name and loads into its context to gain a capability [ 3 ] . These contents are typically organized as a SKILL.md instruction file, optional scripts/ or code blocks, and optional references/ or data files. Because the agent-loaded context is treated as trusted instructions and its scripts run with the agent’s privileges, a poisoned bundle is a direct vehicle for malicious behavior on a coding agent [ 19 , 36 ] . Moreover, the adversary need not concentrate the payload in one place: a natural-language directive in SKILL.md instructs the agent to run a bundled script, while the script itself carries the exfiltration logic, so the malicious intent is split across the two media a skill ships. Despite this exposed surface, offensive research on skills remains thin and largely benchmark- or template-level : existing work measures how often agents follow injected instructions, or supplies hand-written poisoned templates [ 27 , 53 , 50 ] . What is missing is a systematic, software-and-systems account of how an adversary can engineer a skill to defeat the deployed defenses while keeping its payload intact. evidence.excerpt: Agent Skills for Large Language Models: Architecture, Acquisition, Security, and the Path Forward Renjun Xu ReDiscovery Hangzhou China rux@zju.edu.cn and Yang Yan Westlake University Hangzhou China yanyang@westlake.edu.cn (2026) Abstract. The transition from monolithic language models to modular, skill-equipped agents marks a defining shift in how large language models (LLMs) are deployed in practice. Rather than encoding all procedural knowledge within model weights, agent skills—composable packages of instructions, code, and resources that agents load on demand—enable dynamic capability extension without retraining. It is formalized in a paradigm of progressive disclosure, portable skill definitions, and integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This survey provides a comprehensive treatment of the agent skills landscape, as it has rapidly evolved during the last few months. We organize the field along four axes: (i) architectural foundations, examining the SKILL.md specification, progressive context loading, and the complementary roles of skills and MCP; (ii) skill acquisition, covering reinforcement learning with skill libraries (SAGE), autonomous skill discovery (SEAgent), and compositional skill synthesis; (iii) deployment at scale, emphasizing computer-use agents (CUAs) while situating them alongside software-engineering, web, tool-use, and embodied-agent benchmarks; and (iv) security, where recent empirical analyses report that 26.1% of community-contributed skills contain vulnerabilities, motivating our proposed Skill Trust and Lifecycle Governance Framework—a four-tier, gate-based permission model that maps skill provenance to graduated deployment capabilities. We identify seven open challenges—from cross-platform skill portability to capability-based permission models—and propose a research agenda for realizing trustworthy, self-improving skill ecosystems. Unlike prior surveys that broadly cover LLM agents or tool use, this work focuses specifically on the emerging skill abstraction layer and its implications for the next generation of agentic systems. An accompanying collection of agent skills resources is available at https://github.com/scienceaix/agentskills . Introduction The capabilities of large language models have expanded dramatically, yet their utility as autonomous agents remains constrained by a fundamental tension: general-purpose models possess broad knowledge but lack the specialized procedural expertise that real-world tasks demand. Fine-tuning addresses this partially, but at significant cost and with limited composability. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides external knowledge, but the retrieved passages are passive—they cannot prescribe multi-step workflows, bundle executable code, or adapt the agent’s tool permissions at runtime. Agent skills resolve this tension by introducing a modular, filesystem-based abstraction that equips agents with domain-specific expertise on demand. In this paradigm, a skill is not a model or a prompt template, but a self-contained package: a structured instruction file (SKILL.md), optional scripts, reference documents, and assets, organized in a directory that the agent discovers, loads, and follows when relevant tasks arise (Zhang et al. , 2025 ) . The distinction from traditional tools is architectural: tools execute and return results, whereas skills prepare the agent to solve a problem by injecting procedural knowledge, modifying execution context, and enabling progressive disclosure of information. Anthropic formalized this concept in October 2025 with the launch of Agent Skills across Claude’s product surface (Anthropic, 2025e ) , followed by its release as an open standard in December 2025 (Anthropic, 2025a ) . Within four months, the anthropics/skills repository accumulated over 62,000 GitHub stars, partner-built skills from Atlassian, Figma, Canva, Stripe, and Notion entered a curated directory, and structurally identical architectures were independently adopted by other frontier model providers. This rapid convergence reflects a broader recognition: as agents move from research prototypes to production deployments, the industry needs standardized mechanisms for packaging, distributing, and governing procedural expertise. The parallel maturation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—an open standard for connecting agents to external data and tools, donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025 (Anthropic, 2025c ) —provides the complementary infrastructure layer. Together, skills and MCP define an emerging agentic stack in which skills supply the “what to do” and MCP supplies the “how to connect.” This survey is the first to provide a focused treatment of the agent skills paradigm. While excellent surveys exist on LLM agents broadly (Luo and others, 2025 ; Plaat and others, 2025 ) , tool use (Qu and others, 2025 ) , and GUI agents (Zhang and others, 2024 ; Hu and others, 2025 ) , none specifically examines the skill abstraction layer that has emerged as a unifying architectural primitive. Our contributions are: (1) A systematic analysis of the Agent Skills architecture, including progressive disclosure, the SKILL.md specification, and its relationship to MCP (Section 3 ). (2) A taxonomy of skill acquisition methods spanning reinforcement learning, autonomous exploration, compositional synthesis, and human-authored knowledge packaging (Section 4 ). (3) A critical assessment of deployment settings for skills, emphasizing the computer-use agent (CUA) stack while situating it within broader software-engineering, web, function-calling, and embodied-agent evaluation contexts (Section 5 ). (4) The first consolidated treatment of agent skill security, synthesizing three concurrent empirical studies, and an original Skill Trust and Lifecycle Governance Framework that maps acquisition provenance through verification gates to graduated deployment permissions (Section 6 ). (5) An articulation of seven open challenges and a research agenda for the field (Section 7 ). 2. Background and Scope 2.1. From Prompt Engineering to Skill Engineering The evolution toward agent skills can be understood as a progression through three paradigms of LLM capability extension. Prompt engineering (2022–2023) demonstrated that carefully crafted instructions could elicit impressive zero-shot and few-shot behaviors, but prompts are ephemeral, non-modular, and difficult to version or share. Tool use and function calling (2023–2024) enabled models to invoke external APIs, but each tool is atomic—a single function with defined inputs and outputs. Tools execute and return; they do not reshape the agent’s understanding of a task. Skill engineering (2025–present) introduces a higher-order abstraction. A skill is a bundle that can include instructions, workflow guidance, executable scripts, reference documentation, and metadata, all organized to be dynamically loaded when relevant. The key insight is that many real-world tasks require not a single tool call but a coordinated sequence of decisions informed by domain-specific procedural knowledge. A PDF-processing skill, for example, does not merely expose a “fill form” function; it teaches the agent how to approach PDF manipulation, which libraries to use, what edge cases to handle, and what code to execute (Zhang et al. , 2025 ) . 2.2. Relationship to Prior Work Several foundational works anticipated the skill paradigm. Voyager (Wang and others, 2023 ) introduced a skill library for embodied agents in Minecraft, where LLM-generated programs were stored and composed to solve increasingly complex tasks. CREATOR (Qian and others, 2024 ) and Large Language Models as Tool Makers (Cai et al. , 2023 ) explored the idea that LLMs could create their own tools. Toolformer (Schick and others, 2024 ) demonstrated self-taught tool use. However, these works focused on model-generated skills in constrained environments. The Agent Skills paradigm, by contrast, emphasizes human-authored, portable, and governed skill packages designed for production deployment across heterogeneous agent platforms. 2.3.
